screens.title: Oracles and Off-Chain Data
screens.subtitle: How smart contracts securely reach the outside world

narration.text: Smart contracts run in a deterministic, isolated environment and cannot directly read external information like prices, weather, or sports results. That limitation is called the oracle problem and it stops many useful decentralized applications from interacting with real-world events. In this lesson you will learn what an oracle is, the main oracle types you will encounter, and how decentralized networks like Chainlink bridge on-chain logic with off-chain data. We'll use concrete examples such as DeFi price feeds and an example smart contract that reads ETH/USD from a Chainlink feed. You'll also see the risks to avoid — single points of failure, stale feeds, manipulation attempts — and how decentralized oracle networks mitigate those problems by aggregating independent node results. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to explain the oracle problem, pick an appropriate oracle type for a use case, and outline the request/fulfill flow used by Chainlink. Consider a lending protocol that needs a reliable price for collateral; the right oracle design determines whether the protocol is secure and usable. What would you choose for that protocol and why?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Oracles are the trusted bridge between on-chain contracts and off-chain data; decentralized networks reduce single-point risks by aggregating multiple node responses.

screens.title: The Oracle Problem
screens.subtitle: Why blockchains cannot access the real world directly

narration.text: The oracle problem is the fundamental limitation that smart contracts cannot directly read off-chain data. Blockchains are deterministic and isolated: every node must reach the same result from contract execution based only on on-chain state and inputs. If a contract could call arbitrary web APIs during execution, nodes might disagree or face nondeterminism, breaking consensus. This restriction is intentional and keeps the chain secure, but it also prevents many useful DApps from functioning without assistance. For example, a lending protocol needs current market prices to compute collateral ratios. Without an oracle, the contract cannot fetch exchange prices, so it cannot automatically liquidate or settle positions. A common misconception is that oracles create trustless data by themselves; they do not. An oracle introduces an external trust surface — how that trust is structured determines security. A centralized oracle reintroduces a single point of failure, while decentralized oracle networks reduce that risk. Practical takeaway: treat the oracle as part of your security model. Ask: which parties must you trust, and what failure modes would compromise asset safety? The Oracle Problem means the oracle problem is blockchain isolation: smart contracts cannot fetch off-chain data without an external bridge, which creates design and trust decisions.. In practical terms, why blockchains cannot access the real world directly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: The oracle problem is blockchain isolation: smart contracts cannot fetch off-chain data without an external bridge, which creates design and trust decisions.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › The Oracle Problem
What it is
Blockchains are deterministic and cannot directly access external APIs or sensors. This intentional isolation preserves consensus but prevents direct real-world input.
  • Determinism ensures every node computes the same contract result.
  • External calls during execution can introduce nondeterminism and disagreement.
  • Oracles are needed to bring verified off-chain data on-chain in a controlled way.
Concrete example
A DeFi lending contract needs ETH/USD to value collateral. Without an oracle it cannot fetch the current price, preventing automatic margin checks or liquidations.
Misconceptions
An oracle does not magically make data trustless. It moves trust from one place to another. Centralized oracles introduce single points of failure. Decentralized networks reduce but do not eliminate trust assumptions.
Key Takeaway

Design your DApp assuming the oracle is part of the trusted boundary. Choose redundancy and freshness checks for critical flows.

Check your understanding
Describe one scenario where the oracle problem prevents automatic contract behavior, and name one mitigation strategy.

screens.title: What Is a Blockchain Oracle?
screens.subtitle: How an oracle bridges off-chain data to smart contracts

narration.text: A blockchain oracle is a third-party service that retrieves off-chain data and posts it on-chain in a format a smart contract can consume. Think of it as a translator and messenger: it queries an external source, formats and optionally signs the data, and then delivers it so a contract can read a dependable value. Oracles can be simple — a single server that posts a price — or complex networks that aggregate multiple independent sources and nodes. Their role matters across many use cases: DeFi needs reliable price feeds for borrowing decisions; insurance payouts rely on authenticated event data like flight statuses; gaming needs randomness and state updates; supply chain applications require verified sensor readings. A clear misconception is to assume oracles eliminate all trust. They change the trust model and move it to node operators, data sources, and the oracle network design. For engineering decisions, capture the trust assumptions, frequency of updates, and the cost model when choosing an oracle. What Is a Blockchain Oracle? means an oracle fetches, formats, and delivers off-chain data for smart contracts; its design determines the trust and failure characteristics of your dapp.. In practical terms, how an oracle bridges off-chain data to smart contracts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Oracle role
keyIdea.text: An oracle fetches, formats, and delivers off-chain data for smart contracts; its design determines the trust and failure characteristics of your DApp.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › What Is a Blockchain Oracle?
Definition and role
An oracle retrieves external data, optionally validates or signs it, and publishes a result that smart contracts can read and act on. It transforms raw off-chain inputs into deterministic on-chain values.
  • Query an API, sensor, or human source.
  • Format and (optionally) aggregate results to reduce manipulation risk.
  • Deliver a signed or aggregated result in a transaction that a contract can verify or read.
Concrete use case
A stablecoin contract needs a USD price oracle to keep peg logic accurate. The oracle provides frequent, aggregated price snapshots the contract trusts for minting and burning decisions.
Quick comparison
Single-server oracle: simple but single point of failure.
Decentralized oracle network: higher reliability and tamper resistance.
Key Takeaway
An oracle moves trust to its design: pick an oracle architecture that matches your application's tolerance for risk, latency, and cost.

narration.text: Centralized oracles are run by a single operator. They are simple to implement and cheap, but they reintroduce a single point of failure and require you to trust that operator not to be compromised or act maliciously. Decentralized oracle networks, by contrast, use many independent nodes that fetch data and aggregate results. This reduces the chance that a single compromised node can manipulate a feed and improves censorship resistance. However, decentralized systems add complexity: economic incentives, coordination, and potentially higher cost. A common misconception is that decentralization always eliminates trust. It reduces the risk from any single actor but introduces new trust assumptions such as the node selection mechanism, the integrity of data sources, and aggregation logic. For a DeFi price feed where asset custody is on-chain, prefer decentralized feeds. For a low-stakes internal notification system, a centralized oracle may be sufficient. Ask: which failure mode harms users most — an incorrect price or temporary delay? Centralized vs Decentralized Oracles means centralized oracles trade simplicity for trust risk; decentralized oracle networks trade complexity and cost for resilience and tamper resistance.. In practical terms, tradeoffs: simplicity, trust, and resilience. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tradeoff
keyIdea.text: Centralized oracles trade simplicity for trust risk; decentralized oracle networks trade complexity and cost for resilience and tamper resistance.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Centralized vs Decentralized Oracles
Centralized Oracle
Operated by a single entity. Pros: simple, low cost, fast. Cons: single point of failure, trust required.
  • Good for non-critical integrations and internal systems.
  • Not recommended where asset safety depends on data integrity.
Example
A single server posts token prices for a small UI dashboard — acceptable where security risk is low.
Decentralized Oracle Network
Multiple independent nodes fetch data and the network aggregates results to produce a single feed. Pros: resilience, tamper resistance. Cons: higher complexity and cost.
  • Prefer for DeFi and custody-sensitive applications.
  • Aggregation reduces impact of any single malicious or faulty node.
Example
Chainlink price feeds that aggregate multiple node reports to provide a reliable ETH/USD value used by financial contracts.

screens.title: Software, Hardware and Human Oracles
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right data source for the job

narration.text: Oracles differ not just by centralization but by their data sources. Software oracles fetch web APIs, databases, or other blockchains. They are suited to price feeds, exchange tickers, and public web data. Hardware oracles collect readings from physical devices, sensors, or IoT equipment and are used in supply chain and logistics to attest temperature, location, or tamper events. Human oracles rely on trusted individuals or groups to verify subjective or complex events; they can be useful where automated sensors can't reliably interpret context. Each type brings different failure modes: software oracles depend on A P I availability and integrity, hardware oracles require secure device provisioning and attestation, and human oracles require reputation, incentives, and dispute resolution. A common mistake is mixing a cheap data source with a high-stakes decision. If a payment or liquidation is at stake, prefer redundant sources or a decentralized network that aggregates multiple software or hardware inputs. Ask: does my application need authenticity, freshness, or context? That requirement drives the oracle type choice. Software, Hardware and Human Oracles means pick an oracle type based on what data is required: web apis for prices, hardware for physical sensors, and humans for subjective verification.. In practical terms, choosing the right data source for the job. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Source selection
keyIdea.text: Pick an oracle type based on what data is required: web APIs for prices, hardware for physical sensors, and humans for subjective verification.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Software, Hardware and Human Oracles
Software Oracles
Fetch web APIs, databases, or blockchain data. Use for price feeds and public information.
Hardware Oracles
Collect sensor and device readings. Use for supply chain, environmental monitoring, and device attestation.
Human Oracles
Trusted individuals confirm complex or subjective events. Use when machines lack reliable interpretation.
Choosing the right source
Evaluate three properties: authenticity, freshness, and context. A price feed prioritizes freshness and authenticity; a sensor prioritizes physical attestation; a human oracle provides context where rules are fuzzy. When stakes are high, combine sources and aggregate results to reduce manipulation risk.
Use hardware oracles when physical truth is required and devices can be attested.
Use software oracles for frequent, low-latency price updates from trustworthy APIs.

screens.title: Chainlink: Decentralized Oracle Network
screens.subtitle: Core components and how they collaborate to deliver data

narration.text: Chainlink provides a structured way for smart contracts to request external data while reducing single-point failure and manipulation risks. The main components are: requester contracts that emit a request for data, Chainlink oracle nodes that listen for those requests, external adapters inside nodes which call specific APIs or systems, and decentralized data feeds that aggregate multiple node responses. Requester contracts may use a client library to build and send requests. Node operators pick up tasks, call external adapters or APIs, and sign their results before submitting them on-chain. Chainlink can aggregate responses either through on-chain aggregation of multiple transactions or by providing an already aggregated feed contract. This design splits responsibilities: on-chain contracts express intent, nodes fetch and transform data, and the network-layer enforces aggregation and reputation. A misconception is that Chainlink removes all off-chain trust; it reduces dependence on any single node but still assumes honest behavior from a majority of node operators and accurate underlying data sources. Practically, choose Chainlink feeds when high integrity and uptime are required, and review the feed's node composition and update frequency before relying on it in production.

keyIdea.title: Chainlink overview
keyIdea.text: Chainlink coordinates requester contracts, independent nodes, external adapters, and aggregated feeds to provide reliable on-chain data.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Chainlink Architecture
Core components
  • Requester contract: emits a request for external data.
  • Chainlink Oracle nodes: independent operators that fulfill requests.
  • External adapters: node plugins that connect to specific APIs or systems.
  • Decentralized data feeds: aggregated, tamper-resistant contracts that expose a single trusted value.
Practical note
Before relying on a feed, inspect node diversity, update frequency, and any available reputation metrics. Aggregation parameters determine how individual reports are combined into the final value.
Concrete example
An ETH/USD price feed aggregates multiple node reports into a single aggregated answer contract that many consumer contracts subscribe to for consistent pricing.
Key Takeaway
Chainlink separates request logic from node execution and aggregation, lowering the risk of single-node manipulation when used correctly.

screens.title: Chainlink Request and Fulfillment Flow
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lifecycle from request to on-chain result

narration.text: When a smart contract needs external data, it follows a clear request and fulfillment lifecycle. First, the requester contract forms a request and pays any required fee. This request is announced to the oracle network. Independent Chainlink nodes monitor for such requests and evaluate whether to accept the job. Nodes call external adapters or APIs to fetch the requested data. Each node prepares a response and submits a transaction to the blockchain invoking the consumer's fulfillment function or writing to an aggregator. If multiple nodes respond, the network or aggregator contract combines the responses into a single value according to the chosen aggregation method. The consumer contract then reads the aggregated result and proceeds with its logic. A concrete example: a PriceConsumer pays a LINK fee, nodes fetch exchange prices, and an aggregated feed updates the ETH/USD value. A common misconception is that the consumer contract directly receives data instantly; in practice, there is latency for off-chain fetches and on-chain transactions, and nodes must be incentivized to perform work. For design, always consider fee funding, update cadence, and how your contract verifies freshness and origin of results.

keyIdea.title: Flow summary
keyIdea.text: Request -> Node pick-up -> External fetch -> Node submit -> Aggregation -> Consumer reads result. Each step has latency and trust considerations.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Chainlink Request Flow
Request lifecycle
1. Requester creates request and pays fee
2. Nodes detect request and accept job
3. Nodes fetch external API or adapter
4. Nodes submit on-chain responses
5. Aggregation and consumer reads final value
Concrete example
A PriceConsumer requests ETH/USD. Several nodes query exchanges, transform data to the agreed format, and post results. The aggregator contract computes a median or weighted average and stores the latestRoundData for consumers to query.
Design checklist
  • Ensure adequate LINK funding or payment model for requests.
  • Check update cadence vs freshness requirements.
  • Validate timestamps or answered-in-round fields for staleness protection.

screens.title: Using Chainlink Price Feeds (AggregatorV3Interface)
screens.subtitle: Read the latest aggregated price with a Solidity consumer

narration.text: A common and practical way to use Chainlink is with their price feed contracts that implement a standard interface. The AggregatorV3 interface exposes a latestRoundData function which returns a price and a timestamp among other fields. Consumer contracts can call this read-only function without sending LINK or waiting for a callback because the feed contract is already populated by Chainlink nodes. In practice, you import the AggregatorV3 interface, instantiate it with the feed address for your chosen network, and call latestRoundData to get the most recent aggregated answer. For example, an ETH/USD feed often uses eight decimals, so the raw integer needs dividing by ten to the power of eight to be human readable. A misconception is to treat the returned integer as already human friendly. Always check the decimals and timestamp fields to avoid stale or mis-scaled values. The code panel shows a simplified consumer contract used in the lab. Use read-only calls for on-chain price reads when possible to avoid extra gas for callbacks. Using Chainlink Price Feeds (AggregatorV3Interface) means use aggregatorv3interface to query an already-aggregated price feed on-chain; always handle decimals and timestamps for accuracy.. In practical terms, read the latest aggregated price with a solidity consumer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Aggregator usage
keyIdea.text: Use AggregatorV3Interface to query an already-aggregated price feed on-chain; always handle decimals and timestamps for accuracy.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Price Feed Example
Simplified PriceConsumerV3
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

import "@chainlink/contracts/src/v0.8/interfaces/AggregatorV3Interface.sol";

contract PriceConsumerV3 {
  AggregatorV3Interface internal priceFeed;

  constructor(address feed) {
    priceFeed = AggregatorV3Interface(feed);
  }

  function getLatestPrice() public view returns (int) {
    (, int price, , ,) = priceFeed.latestRoundData();
    return price; // Remember: apply decimals when making UI-ready values
  }
}
Example notes
Provide the correct feed address for your network. The returned price is an integer scaled by the feed's decimals, typically eight for ETH/USD. Convert it in the frontend or contract as needed.
Key Takeaway
Use read-only Aggregator calls to obtain aggregated prices without submitting new transactions when possible; check decimals and timestamps.

screens.title: Requesting Custom API Data (APIConsumer Pattern)
screens.subtitle: How ChainlinkClient-based requests are built, sent, and fulfilled

narration.text: For arbitrary A P I requests you use the ChainlinkClient pattern. The contract builds a request object that specifies the job identifier, the target endpoint, and how to extract a path from the JSON response. The contract pays a LINK fee and calls sendChainlinkRequest which creates an on-chain request that node operators can see. A node picks up the task, performs the external A P I call through an adapter, and then calls back on-chain to the consumer's fulfill function with the result. In practice you must provide a valid job ID from a node operator, fund the contract with LINK tokens, and implement a safe fulfill function that validates the responder and protects against reentrancy. A common safety mistake is assuming any on-chain callback is safe; the fulfill function must use access control or record the requestId to verify the origin and avoid reentrancy issues. The code comment block in this panel outlines the pattern and the minimum payment and setup steps required before sending requests. Requesting Custom API Data (APIConsumer Pattern) means build a chainlink request with jobid, endpoint, and path; fund the contract with link and validate fulfill callbacks carefully to avoid security issues.. In practical terms, how chainlinkclient-based requests are built, sent, and fulfilled. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: APIConsumer pattern
keyIdea.text: Build a Chainlink request with jobId, endpoint, and path; fund the contract with LINK and validate fulfill callbacks carefully to avoid security issues.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › APIConsumer Pattern
Pattern overview
/* Pseudocode outline
import ChainlinkClient

constructor() { setPublicChainlinkToken(...); jobId = "YOUR_JOB"; fee = 0.1 * 10**18; }

function requestPrice(symbol) public returns (bytes32) {
  build request with jobId, add "get" endpoint, add "path" for JSON
  return sendChainlinkRequest(request, fee);
}

function fulfill(requestId, price) public recordChainlinkFulfillment(requestId) {
  currentPrice = price;
}
*/
Operational notes
You must fund the contract with LINK tokens and configure the jobId and node operator. Ensure your fulfill function protects against reentrancy and checks the originating requestId.
Key Takeaway
API requests require node operators and LINK payment. Treat callbacks as external transactions and validate them carefully.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Considerations
screens.subtitle: What to avoid and how to harden your oracle integration

narration.text: Security and operational issues with oracles are common yet avoidable when you apply a checklist mindset. First, avoid single points of failure by preferring decentralized feeds for critical on-chain decisions. Second, guard against stale data by checking timestamps or round identifiers returned by feeds and refusing to act on data older than your policy allows. Third, expect attempts to manipulate small or poorly aggregated sources; use aggregation, median, or weighted schemes and diverse data sources to reduce manipulation risk. Fourth, be mindful of gas costs: oracle fulfillments are on-chain transactions that require gas; ensure payment and economic incentives align for node operators. Fifth, craft fulfill functions defensively: validate caller identity, verify request identifiers, and minimize external calls to prevent reentrancy. Finally, document your trust assumptions: which node operators, data sources, or adapters you rely on and why. A mistaken belief is that decentralization alone solves all problems; it lowers some risks but requires careful configuration and ongoing monitoring. The takeaway: design oracle usage as part of your security perimeter and test failure modes before production deployment. Common Mistakes and Safety Considerations means avoid single points of failure, check for stale data, use aggregation, fund gas and link properly, and validate fulfill callbacks to reduce operational and security risks.. In practical terms, what to avoid and how to harden your oracle integration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safety checklist
keyIdea.text: Avoid single points of failure, check for stale data, use aggregation, fund gas and LINK properly, and validate fulfill callbacks to reduce operational and security risks.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Common Mistakes & Safety
Common mistakes
  • Using a single centralized oracle for critical financial decisions.
  • Not checking timestamps or round identifiers, leading to stale data usage.
  • Failing to validate fulfill caller identity and requestId, opening up malicious callbacks.
  • Underfunding LINK or ignoring gas costs required for node fulfillments.
Mitigations
Use decentralized feeds, add staleness checks, require multiple sources, secure fulfill functions, and monitor feed health and node diversity.
Pro tip
Record and verify the requestId on send and check it inside fulfill to ensure the callback corresponds to your request.
Warning

Relying on a single data source for high-value logic reintroduces trust and attack risk. Use aggregation for safety.

screens.title: Deploying PriceConsumer to Testnet
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step deployment checklist and expected outcome

narration.text: This activity walks you through deploying a PriceConsumer contract on a testnet and reading the latest ETH/USD price. Start with a Hardhat project and install the Chainlink contracts package. Add PriceConsumerV3. sol into your contracts directory and ensure the constructor points to a valid feed address for the chosen testnet. Compile with the recommended Solidity version, configure the sepolia or preferred network with an RPC provider key and a funded account, and add the Chainlink feed ABI if required by your toolchain. Deploy using a deployment script and capture the resulting contract address. In the Hardhat console or a simple script, attach to the deployed contract and call getLatestPrice. You should receive an integer that represents the price scaled by the feed's decimals, commonly eight. Convert this integer by dividing by ten to the power of the feed decimals or use a utility in your frontend library. Expected outcome: a deployed contract address and the printed scaled price. Common pitfalls: wrong feed address, insufficient testnet funds for gas, or forgetting to compile with correct solidity pragma. After completing the steps, reflect: did the returned timestamp and decimals meet your freshness and format expectations?

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Deploy a PriceConsumer on a testnet, call getLatestPrice, and convert the scaled integer into a human-readable price.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Deploy PriceConsumer
Deployment checklist
  1. Install @chainlink/contracts in your project.
  2. Add PriceConsumerV3.sol with the correct feed address for your network.
  3. Compile, configure Hardhat network with RPC key and private key, fund testnet account.
  4. Run deploy script and copy the deployed address.
  5. Attach in console and call getLatestPrice, then convert using feed decimals.
Expected output
A deployed contract address and a printed integer representing the scaled price. Use formatUnits or divide by ten to the feed decimals to display the human price.
Common pitfalls
Wrong feed address, insufficient gas, wrong compiler version, or forgetting to fund LINK when using job-based requests.
Why it matters
Seeing the live feed confirms your contract can trust and act on external data — a fundamental capability for many DApps.

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts to remember. First: the oracle problem — blockchains are isolated and need external bridges to access real-world data. Second: a blockchain oracle is the bridge that brings external data on-chain, but it also brings trust assumptions that must be examined. Third: prefer decentralized oracle networks for critical financial applications because they aggregate multiple independent nodes and reduce the chance of manipulation. Fourth: Chainlink provides requester contracts, independent node operators, external adapters, and aggregated feeds to structure off-chain to on-chain data delivery. Fifth: when using price feeds, always handle feed decimals and verify timestamps to avoid stale data. Keep these concepts in mind as the checklist when designing any DApp that depends on off-chain information. Which single assumption in your design would cause the most harm if it were wrong?

Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Key Concepts
Oracle Problem
Smart contracts cannot directly access external APIs or sensors, limiting on-chain logic unless bridged.
Blockchain Oracle
A service that fetches off-chain data, formats it, and delivers it for contract consumption.
Decentralized Oracle Network
A network of nodes that fetch and aggregate data, reducing single-node risk for critical applications.
Summary Takeaway

Treat oracle choice as a core security decision: prefer aggregated, decentralized feeds for high-value logic and always validate freshness and format.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three final cards to keep in mind

narration.text: Close the chapter by holding three short, actionable reminders. First: design for trust boundaries — when you add an oracle you add new parties and assumptions. Second: prefer aggregated, decentralized feeds for any operation that affects user funds or custody. Third: always verify format and freshness — check decimals, timestamps, and round identifiers before acting on feed values. These three checkpoints will help you choose the right oracle approach and avoid common errors like stale or manipulated data or improper callback handling. As you apply this knowledge, document the assumptions and monitor your chosen feeds for health metrics. Which of these three checkpoints will you verify first in your own DApp?
